title: Message Queues & Async
subtitle: Stop making the user wait for work they don't need to watch
objectives: Decide what work belongs in the request and what belongs behind a queue
Explain how a queue decouples producer from consumer and absorbs spikes
Reason about delivery guarantees and why consumers must be idempotent
Handle the failures: retries, poison messages, ordering, and a backlog you can't drain

lessons.title: Work the user shouldn't wait for

exercises.prompt: A user signs up. Your handler creates the account (20ms), then sends a welcome email via a third-party API (2 seconds). How long do they stare at a spinner?
choices: Over 2 seconds — they're waiting on an email they aren't even looking at
It happens in the background automatically
exercises.why: The response can't return until the handler finishes, so the user waits for every line of it — including a slow call to a service they'll never see the result of. Worse, you've coupled signup's availability to the email provider's: if that API is down, your handler fails and nobody can sign up at all, over an email.

exercises.prompt: A message ______ lets you hand off work now and have it performed later by a separate process.
exercises.why: You write the job down somewhere durable and return immediately; something else picks it up and does it. The user's request stops being 'do the work' and becomes 'record that the work is needed'.

exercises.prompt: Order what happens when signup sends the welcome email asynchronously.
steps: Server puts a 'send welcome email' message on the queue
Server responds — user is done in ~25ms
A worker picks the message up and calls the email API
exercises.why: The user's request now ends the moment the job is recorded, and the slow part happens on someone else's clock. Note the ordering that matters: the response goes out BEFORE the email is sent, which is precisely the trade — the user gets 25ms, and in exchange the email is a promise rather than a fact.

exercises.prompt: Which of these belong behind a queue? Select all.
exercises.why: Emails, reports, and video encoding are slow, the user isn't watching the result, and a few seconds' delay costs nothing. The password check is the opposite on every count: the user is waiting on that exact answer, and deferring it is meaningless because there's nothing to return without it. The test is simply whether the user needs the result to continue.

exercises.prompt: What have you given up by moving the email to a queue?
choices: Certainty at response time: you told the user 'done' when the email is merely scheduled, so if it later fails, they've already been told it worked
exercises.why: Async converts a synchronous fact into a promise — at the moment you respond, the work has not happened, and you're asserting it will. That's fine for a welcome email and unacceptable for 'your payment succeeded', so the question is always what happens if this promise is broken and nobody's watching. Answer it before you defer the work, not during the incident.

exercises.prompt: Beyond speed, what does the queue give you when the email provider goes down for an hour?
choices: Signups keep working, and the messages wait in the queue until the provider returns
The queue sends the emails itself
exercises.why: The queue is a buffer between two systems that no longer have to be healthy at the same moment — a dead provider stops emails from being SENT without stopping them from being ACCEPTED. That decoupling is often worth more than the latency win: the failure of a non-essential dependency stops taking down an essential path.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of a queue system.

pairs.right: Takes messages off and does the work
Durable storage for work not yet done

exercises.why: Producers and consumers never speak to each other — they only touch the queue, which is what lets them be deployed, scaled, and broken independently. The acknowledgement is the load-bearing piece: without it the queue can't distinguish 'done' from 'the worker died holding it'.

exercises.prompt: Black Friday: uploads spike to 10× normal, far beyond what your video encoders can handle. With a queue in front, what happens?
choices: Uploads are accepted quickly and the queue grows; workers keep chewing through at their own pace, so the backlog absorbs the spike instead of the users feeling it
exercises.why: A queue turns a spike in arrival rate into a spike in queue DEPTH rather than a spike in failures, which is the whole reason to buffer: the users' side stays fast and the backlog just gets longer for a while. That only works if the average rate is sustainable, though — a buffer smooths bursts, and nothing can smooth a permanent excess.

exercises.prompt: Your queue depth has been growing steadily for six hours. What does that mean?
choices: The buffer is working as intended
Arrivals are outpacing your workers — this isn't a burst being absorbed, it's a deficit compounding, and it will never recover on its own
exercises.why: A queue absorbing a burst rises and then falls; a queue that only rises means arrival rate exceeds service rate, and no amount of waiting fixes that — the gap compounds every second. Depth is therefore your key signal, and its DERIVATIVE is what matters: rising and returning is healthy, monotonically rising means add workers or shed load, now.

exercises.prompt: How do you make the backlog drain faster?
choices: Add more consumers — they pull from the same queue independently, and that's exactly the workload that scales horizontally
exercises.why: Queued work is usually the ideal horizontal case from unit 11: each message is independent, so two workers never coordinate and ten workers do ten times the work. A bigger queue just gives you more room to fall behind — it changes when you notice the problem, not whether you have one.

exercises.prompt: A worker crashes halfway through processing a message. What should the queue do?
choices: Delete the message — it was delivered
Give it to another worker, since it was never acknowledged and therefore was never completed
Retry only if the worker asks
Log an error and move on
exercises.why: This is exactly why acknowledgement exists: the queue holds the message as in-flight and only deletes it when a worker confirms success, so a crash means the ack never arrives and the message becomes available again. That in-flight message is state the system must not lose — the same point unit 5 made about work-in-progress — and it's why real queues persist messages to disk rather than holding them in memory.

exercises.prompt: Does adding a queue make the overall work finish sooner?
choices: No — the same work still happens, and the total takes slightly longer with the extra hop. What changed is who waits: the user doesn't
exercises.why: The encoding still takes its two minutes; you've moved it off the user's clock, not shortened it. This is unit 4's split, sharpened: async improves perceived latency and throughput under bursts while slightly worsening end-to-end latency for the task itself — which is a superb trade exactly when nobody is watching the task.

exercises.prompt: A worker finishes the job, then crashes before sending its acknowledgement. What happens to that message?
choices: It's gone — the work was done
The queue never heard 'done', so it redelivers — and the job runs a second time
The queue detects the work completed
It goes to an error log
exercises.why: The queue can only observe acknowledgements, not outcomes, so 'work done but unacked' and 'worker died before starting' look identical from outside — and it must assume the pessimistic one. That gap is unavoidable rather than a bug in any particular queue: there's no way to make finishing the work and confirming it a single atomic act across two machines.

exercises.prompt: Match each delivery guarantee to what it means.
exercises.why: You're choosing which failure to accept: ack before working risks losing the job, ack after working risks doing it twice. Almost every real queue defaults to at-least-once because losing work is usually worse than repeating it — which quietly makes duplicate handling your problem.

exercises.prompt: Your queue is at-least-once. Your worker charges a credit card. What must be true?
choices: The worker must be idempotent: processing the same message twice must charge the customer once
exercises.why: At-least-once means the duplicate isn't a rare accident, it's a documented behaviour that will happen — so a non-idempotent worker on a durable queue is a billing incident waiting for a network blip. For a charge specifically, the fix has to reach the payment provider: derive a stable idempotency key from the message id and pass it in the API call, so the provider collapses the duplicate. A local 'already processed' table isn't enough here — your record and the charge are two different systems, so a crash after the charge but before the record leaves redelivery seeing nothing and charging again. That's the dual-write problem lesson 4 is about, and it's why a local dedup table only works when the record and the effect land in the same transaction, which a third-party charge never does.

exercises.prompt: Vendors advertise 'exactly-once delivery'. What's actually going on?
choices: Delivery can't truly be exactly-once across a network, so what's offered is at-least-once delivery plus deduplication — exactly-once EFFECTS, not exactly-once delivery
It only works for small messages
exercises.why: The message may genuinely arrive twice; the system just remembers it saw that id and discards the repeat, which is deduplication wearing a better name. That's a real and useful feature, with real limits — the dedup window is finite, and it only covers the queue's own boundary, so a side effect your worker performs on a third party is still yours to make idempotent.

exercises.prompt: A message fails, gets retried, fails again — forever. It's blocking the queue and filling your logs. What's it called and what's the fix?
choices: A poison message: after N attempts, move it to a dead-letter queue so it stops consuming capacity and can be inspected
exercises.why: Some messages can never succeed — malformed payloads, a referenced row that's been deleted — and retrying them forever burns capacity while hiding the failure in noise. A dead-letter queue bounds the damage by giving up after N attempts and setting the message aside intact, which turns an infinite loop into a queue you can actually go and look at.

exercises.prompt: Your worker retries a failed message immediately, in a tight loop. The downstream service is already struggling. What have you built?
choices: A hammer: your retries add load to the exact service that's failing, so the retries are now part of why it can't recover
exercises.why: Immediate retries mean a struggling dependency gets MORE traffic precisely when it needs less, and every retry makes recovery less likely — the classic retry storm. Exponential backoff with jitter is the fix: wait longer after each failure, and randomize so a thousand workers don't retry in perfect unison, which was the 429 lesson from unit 2 now applied on your own side of the wire.

exercises.prompt: Two messages for the same user: 'update email to A', then 'update email to B'. Your five workers process them in parallel. What can happen?
choices: B can land before A, leaving the email as A — the older value wins, permanently
Both are applied, ending at B
exercises.why: Parallel workers give you no ordering: two messages in flight at once finish whenever they finish, and 'last write wins' means whichever finishes last, not whichever was sent last. Concurrency bought throughput and spent ordering — and the corruption is silent, since nothing errors and the row just holds a stale value forever.

exercises.prompt: You need those two updates to stay in order. What's the standard approach?
choices: Partition by a key — route all messages for a given user to the same partition, so that user's messages are ordered while different users still process in parallel
exercises.why: Global ordering means one consumer and no parallelism at all, which throws away the reason you queued the work. Per-key ordering is the useful compromise: order is only guaranteed where you actually need it, and unrelated users remain fully parallel. Note this is unit 15's shard key wearing another hat — you're choosing what must be co-located to stay consistent.

exercises.prompt: Your worker updates the database, then publishes a message. It crashes in between. What's broken?
choices: The database change happened but the message never went out, so every downstream system is permanently unaware — and there's no error anywhere
exercises.why: A database transaction and a queue publish are two systems, so unit 9's boundary applies: you cannot make both happen atomically by wrapping them in a `BEGIN`. This is the dual-write problem, and the usual answer is the transactional outbox — write the message into a table inside the same transaction as your data change, then have a separate process read that table and publish. One atomic write, and publishing becomes at-least-once delivery from a durable record.

exercises.prompt: Which are real costs of moving work behind a queue? Select all.
choices: Debugging spans two systems and a time gap
exercises.why: Duplicates come from at-least-once, ordering is surrendered to parallelism, and failures now happen minutes later in a different process with no user waiting to notice — you have to go looking. The user's request gets FASTER, which is the whole point; you paid for it in complexity that lives entirely on your side.

exercises.prompt: A user clicks 'export my data'. Generating it takes about 90 seconds. Slide toward your design.
exercises.rightLabel: Queue it and notify when ready (async, more moving parts)
exercises.why: Ninety seconds is far past where a request should live: the browser or a proxy will likely time out, a retry starts the whole job again, and one slow export holds a connection and a worker hostage. Queue it, return 'we'll email you', and the work runs where nothing is waiting on it — the extra machinery is worth it the moment the task outlives a reasonable request.

exercises.prompt: Your queue backlog is 4 million messages and workers are at max. Adding workers hits the database's write limit. What now?
choices: The bottleneck moved downstream — the queue was never the constraint, so you must shed load, batch the writes, or scale the database
exercises.why: The queue faithfully absorbed everything and handed the problem to the next stage: your real limit is the database's write rate, and unit 4's rule says capacity added anywhere but the bottleneck buys nothing. That's the queue's dark side — it hides a capacity deficit behind a growing number instead of failing loudly, so you discover the true constraint with four million messages of debt already accrued.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of queues?
choices: They make systems faster and more reliable automatically
They take work off the user's clock and decouple systems that shouldn't fail together — and charge you in duplicates, lost ordering, delayed failures, and backlogs that hide a deficit
They're only for very large systems
They guarantee work is never lost
exercises.why: A queue converts a synchronous fact into a durable promise, which is exactly what buys the speed and the decoupling — and exactly what creates every cost. The promise can be fulfilled twice, out of order, much later, or pile up unfulfilled, and none of those failures has a user watching to report them. That's the trade: the user stops waiting, and you take on the job of making sure the promise is kept.
